n: Paul turns to another question from their letter: spiritual gifts. He wants them to understand these properly.
Before conversion, they were swept along in the worship of lifeless idols that couldn’t speak — sometimes in emotional frenzy.
Here’s the test: no one speaking by God’s Spirit curses Jesus, and no one can truly confess Jesus as Lord except by the Holy Ghost.
There are many kinds of gifts, but one Spirit gives them all.
There are different kinds of service, but the same Lord directs them.
There are different ways God works, but the same God works through them all. Spirit, Lord, and God — Paul mentions all three members of the Godhead.
Each person receives some manifestation of the Spirit — for the benefit of everyone, not just for personal display.
One receives the gift to speak with wisdom, another to speak with knowledge — both by the same Spirit.

f.g: Here, inspired wise counsel — not the Latter-day Saint health code (D&C 89), which shares the name.

n: Another receives exceptional faith; another gifts of healing.
Others receive the gifts of miracles, prophecy, discerning spirits, speaking in tongues, and interpreting tongues.

f.g: Various languages — inspired speech in a language unknown to the speaker.

n: All these come from the same Spirit, who distributes them to each person as He chooses.
Paul compares the Church to a human body: many parts, one body. So it is with Christ’s body.
Through one Spirit all were baptized into one body — Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free — and all drink from that same Spirit.
A body isn’t one part — it is many.

f.g: Diversity is built into the design.

n: If a foot said, “I’m not a hand, so I don’t belong,” it would still be part of the body. Feeling less important doesn’t make you less needed.

f.w: I am not of the body
f.g: Paul speaks to members who feel their gifts don’t count.

n: Same with an ear that wishes it were an eye — it still belongs.

f.g: A body part that seems less noticeable than the eye.

n: If the whole body were an eye, how would it hear? If it were all ear, how would it smell? Every function matters.

f.g: The body would lose essential abilities.

n: God Himself has placed each part in the body exactly as He chose.
If everyone were the same part, there would be no body at all.
So there are many parts, yet one body.
Now Paul speaks to those who feel superior: the eye can’t say it doesn’t need the hand, nor the head the feet.

f.w: I have no need of thee
f.g: The attitude of proud members toward others.

n: In fact, the parts that seem weakest are indispensable.

f.g: Like internal organs — hidden but vital.

n: We give special care and covering to parts we consider less presentable.

f.g: Less presentable parts, which we modestly clothe.

n: Our presentable parts need no special treatment. God arranged the body to give more honor to the parts that lacked it.
So there would be no division in the body, but all parts would care for one another equally.
When one part hurts, the whole body hurts. When one part is honored, all rejoice.

f.w: all the members suffer with it

n: The Corinthian saints are Christ’s body, and each is an individual part of it.
God placed in the Church apostles first, then prophets, then teachers, followed by other gifts and roles. Latter-day Saints see this order restored in the Church today.
Are all apostles or prophets or teachers or miracle workers? Obviously not.

f.g: The questions in Greek expect the answer “no.”

n: Not all heal, speak in tongues, or interpret. The Corinthians overvalued tongues; Paul shows it is only one gift among many.
Seek earnestly the greater gifts. But Paul is about to show them something even more excellent: charity.
